new_statements.locator: pp. 66-67, section 3.1 'Phonemes' (last paragraph of p. 66 and the example block at the top of p. 67); PDF pages 6-7 of the copy consulted
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (34 pp., no text; extracted text yields 34 chars) and its scanned companion. Rendered PDF pages 6-7 (printed pp. 66-67) to PNG and read the passage from the page scan itself, not only the scanned. Verbatim at the stated locator: last paragraph of p. 66, section 3.1 Phonemes: "Stress in Bobongko is predictably penultimate, with suffixation precipitating stress movement. Compare the two following word pairs:" followed at the top of p. 67 (under the running head "A preliminary Sketch of the Bobongko Language") by the four-line example block duangan [duˈaŋan] 'boat' / duanganto [duaˈŋanto] 'our boat' / konyuku [koˈɲuku] 'fingernail' / konyukuung [koɲuˈkuːŋ] 'your fingernail', exactly as…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; when a suffix or enclitic is added, stress shifts rightward so that it stays on the new penult (du'angan -> dua'nganto; ko'nyuku -> konyu'kuung). A final diphthong (-oy) counts as one syllable for the count.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The only related remark (p. 67) is that penultimate stress on lumangoy 'swim' shows the final -oy to be a diphthong rather than two vowels, i.e. the rule is used to decide syllabification, not as an exception. The author (p. 61) calls the whole paper preliminary, based on one week of fieldwork in January 2001.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level; the examples are isolated citation forms, stem versus stem+suffix/enclitic (possessive -to 'our', -ung 'your'). The rule is stated for the phonological word including suffixes, hence 'stress movement' under suffixation.
new_statements.identity_note: Mead 2001 describes the Bobongko of Lembanato village (Kilat Bay, Togian Island), the main community; the same language as Glottolog bobo1255 / ISO bgb. No dialect split is described; a splinter community at Tumbulawa (Batu Daka Island) is mentioned but not separately documented.

new_statements.quote: Klemtoon. Het Bobongko'sch heeft den klemtoon op de voorlaatste lettergreep van elk woord; bij samenstelling of aanhechting van achtervoegsels verspringt dus de klemtoon van de voorlaatste lettergreep van 't grondwoord naar de voorlaatste van het samengestelde woord, bijv. Súsu, susúnjo; bája, bajánjo; antáta, antatámo; mále, malémo; búto, butóngku; sangálu sangelúum. Daar voorvoegsels het accent niet veranderen, blijft de klemtoon van een éénlettergrepigen stam, die alleen met voorvoegsels is samengesteld op het stamwoord, dus op de laatste lettergreep van het afgeleide woord, bijv. mendî „baden", van di; mongkân „eten", van kan; mompokotû „wonen," van tu; pinotû, opotû „dier, huisdier," van denzelfden stam.
new_statements.translation: Stress. Bobongko has the stress on the penultimate syllable of every word; in compounding or attachment of suffixes the stress therefore shifts from the penultimate syllable of the base word to the penultimate of the compound word, e.g. súsu, susúnjo; bája, bajánjo; antáta, antatámo; mále, malémo; búto, butóngku; sangálu sangelúum. Since prefixes do not change the accent, the stress of a monosyllabic stem that is compounded with prefixes only stays on the stem word, thus on the last syllable of the derived word, e.g. mendî 'to bathe', from di; mongkân 'to eat', from kan; mompokotû 'to dwell', from tu; pinotû, opotû 'animal, domestic animal', from the same stem.
new_statements.citation: Adriani, N. 1900. De talen der Togian-eilanden. Tijdschrift voor Indische Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde 42: 428-490, 539-566.

Read the page scan and : the passage is there verbatim as quoted, including the diacritics the scanned garbles (image: 'Súsu, susúnjo; bája, bajánjo; antáta, antatámo; mále, malémo; bút…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog (penultimate stress = penultimate) and as Mead 2001:66-67 ('predictably penultimate, with suffixation precipitating stress movement'). Adds detail the catalog and Mead 2001 lack: prefixes do not count, so prefixed monosyllabic roots are final-stressed (a morphologically conditioned exception, not a different type). The PDF's second 'Klemtoon' section (offprint pp. 45-46) concerns Badjo'sch (Bajau/Sama, dialects M. and T.), not Bobongko, and is not used here.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of every word, counted on the whole word including suffixes (suffixation moves the stress rightward). Prefixes never move the stress, so a monosyllabic root that carries only prefixes keeps the stress on the root, which is then the final syllable of the derived word.
new_statements.exceptions: Prefixed monosyllabic roots keep root (= final-syllable) stress: mendî 'bathe' (< di), mongkân 'eat' (< kan), mompokotû 'dwell', pinotû, opotû (< tu). The circumflex marks these final stressed vowels; no other exceptions given.
new_statements.identity_note: Adriani 1900 describes the Bobongko'sch of the Togian Islands as spoken in 1900 (the part of the article read is the Batavia 1900 offprint of part 1, TBG 42: 428-490). The same offprint contains a second 'Klemtoon' section (offprint pp. 45-46) about Badjo'sch (Bajau/Sama) dialects M. and T. of the Togian Islands, which is a different language and was not used. The listed HathiTrust item uc1.31822038199519 is the same offprint ('De talen der Togian-Eilanden / door N. Adriani', rights pd, Full view per the catalog API) but babel.hathitrust.org blocks our network's IP; the copy read is the KB/Delpher digitization (Utrecht UB MAG: PKF 1136) found through the KB SRU catalogue.
